parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State the magnitude and unit of absolute zero on the thermodynamic temperature scale.
hints: Hint 1: Think about the starting point of the Kelvin scale. What is the lowest possible temperature where particles have minimum internal energy?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remember What Thermodynamic Means**
The thermodynamic scale, the Kelvin scale, does not depend on any particular substance. Its zero is the true physical zero, the temperature at which all thermal motion stops and no more energy can be removed.

Step 2: **State Absolute Zero**
That point is defined as: $$T = 0\text{ K}$$ There is no negative temperature on this scale.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Explain why temperature measured using a laboratory liquid-in-glass thermometer does **not** give a measurement of thermodynamic temperature.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what actually expands in a liquid-in-glass thermometer and whether every liquid would expand in exactly the same way.
parts.proper_answer: The measured temperature depends on the properties of the thermometric substance, e.g. the thermal expansion of the particular liquid and glass, so it is not independent of the substance and is not thermodynamic temperature.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What a Liquid-in-Glass Thermometer Really Measures**
You are not measuring temperature directly. You are measuring length of a liquid column. You then assume a certain expansion behaviour to convert length to temperature.

Step 2: **Why This Is Not Thermodynamic**
Thermodynamic temperature must be the same no matter what substance is used. But different liquids expand differently, and glass also expands. So two thermometers with different liquids would disagree slightly. The reading depends on the properties of the liquid and glass used.

hints: Hint 1: Look carefully at the shape and slope of the graph in Fig. 2.2. What does the steady upward slope tell you about how $\rho$ responds when $T$ increases?
Hint 2: For a good thermometer you need easy calibration and no confusion between two temperatures. What does a straight line with no flat parts or turning points give you?
parts.proper_answer: Resistivity varies with temperature, giving a usable thermometric property. The variation is linear (straight-line graph) and each value of resistivity corresponds to one unique temperature, allowing simple calibration.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **A Property That Changes With Temperature**
Fig. 2.2 shows $\rho$ increases steadily as $T$ increases. Because resistance $R$ is proportional to $\rho$, measuring $R$ between X and Y tells you about $T$. That makes resistivity a suitable thermometric property.

Step 2: **Why Linear and Unique Matters**
The graph is a straight line. That means: $$\rho \propto T \text{ (linear)}$$ A linear change is easy to calibrate with just two fixed points. Also the line keeps rising with no maximum or minimum, so every $\rho$ value means one and only one $T$. There is no ambiguity.

parts.text: Suggest a reason why a platinum resistance thermometer is **not** suitable for measuring a rapidly changing temperature.

thermometer takes time to reach the correct

hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 2.1. Think about the size of the glass tube, plastic strip and wire. What must happen thermally before the platinum wire is at the new temperature?
parts.proper_answer: The thermometer has a large heat capacity / large mass so significant energy transfer is needed for it to reach thermal equilibrium with the surroundings, giving a slow response time.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Big Thermometer Needs Lots of Heating**
Look at Fig. 2.1. There is a large glass tube plus a plastic strip plus the wire. That is a lot of material with a large total heat capacity.

Step 2: **Slow to Reach Equilibrium**
When the outside temperature changes quickly, heat must flow to or from all that glass and plastic before the platinum reaches the new temperature. That energy transfer takes time, so the thermometer lags behind a rapidly changing temperature.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Suggest a type of thermometer that is suitable for measuring a rapidly changing temperature.
hints: Hint 1: Think about which electrical thermometer uses just a tiny junction of two wires with almost no mass to heat up.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **A Tiny Sensor Responds Fast**
A thermocouple is just two thin wires joined at a small junction. Its mass and heat capacity are very small, so it reaches thermal equilibrium almost instantly.

Step 2: **Best Choice Here**
Because it has very low thermal inertia and gives an electrical e.m.f. that follows temperature quickly, a thermocouple is suitable for rapidly changing temperatures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
A negative temperature coefficient thermistor may be used as a type of resistance thermometer.

State **one** way in which the variation with temperature of the resistance of a thermistor differs from that of a platinum wire.
hints: Hint 1: Recall what NTC means for how resistance moves when temperature rises, and compare the shape of that curve to the straight rising line for platinum in Fig. 2.2.
parts.proper_answer: For an NTC thermistor resistance decreases as temperature increases (inverse variation) and the variation is non-linear, whereas for platinum resistance increases linearly with temperature.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Opposite Direction**
NTC means negative temperature coefficient. Heating frees more charge carriers, so resistance falls. Platinum is a metal, so heating increases lattice vibrations and resistance rises. The directions are opposite.

Step 2: **Different Shape**
Platinum gives the straight line in Fig. 2.2. An NTC thermistor gives a curved, non-linear fall, steep at low $T$ and flattening at high $T$. So one difference is either the inverse sense or the non-linear shape.
